items.ig_caption:
Patch goes in. Exploit comes out. No human. 🤖

What BleepingComputer and SiliconANGLE reported (16 Nov) from Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG):
→ For the first time, GTIG saw threat actors use LLM frameworks to fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation, with no human in the loop
→ It found an exposed attacker staging server running a multi-agent framework dubbed exploit_agent
→ The agents compare web app code before and after each patch announcement, draft an exploit for a likely flaw and run it automatically
→ Targets were French media, entertainment and education websites
→ GTIG expects unsophisticated attacks needing "little to no human interaction" in the next three months

My take: your patch window is now your exposure window. I'd set separate SLAs: internet-facing apps patched in days, and I'd hunt for exploitation of anything patched in the last month.

What to do: shorten patch SLAs for exposed web apps, track new fixes against your internet-facing inventory, and watch for exploitation right after patch releases.

items.take: Your vendor's update server is part of your attack surface. I'd ask critical suppliers how updates are signed and checked, and stage their updates on a test system before production.

cover.hook: A malicious file on a drone maker's update server. Germany's army grounded its drones.
cover.sub: Quantum Systems confirmed "an active cyberattack by hostile actors". The Bundeswehr grounded its Vector drones as a precaution.

slides.title: What was hit
slides.body: German drone maker Quantum Systems confirmed a cyberattack on 12 Nov, identified at the end of October. Per Der Spiegel, as relayed by several outlets, a malicious file was placed on the server that distributes QBase updates, its ground-control software.

slides.label: customer grounded its fleet: the Bundeswehr
slides.note: "The Bundeswehr was the only customer to ground their systems as a precaution." (Quantum spokesperson, via AeroTime)

slides.title: What we don't know
slides.body: Quantum shared no technical details and named no attacker. Security Affairs says it is not clear how many customers installed the file. Quantum says the fleet is flying normally; per AeroTime the Bundeswehr has not independently confirmed that.

slides.title: Do this week
items: Verify signatures before installing vendor updates
Stage updates on a test system first
List vendors that can push code to you
Keep a rollback path for critical software

slides.title: My take
slides.body: Your vendor's update server is part of your attack surface. I'd ask critical suppliers how updates are signed and checked, and stage their updates on a test system before production.

items.ig_caption:
A malicious file on a drone maker's update server. Germany's army grounded its drones. 🛩️

What was reported (Security Affairs 16 Nov, AeroTime 13 Nov):
→ German drone maker Quantum Systems confirmed "an active cyberattack by hostile actors", identified at the end of October
→ Per Der Spiegel, as relayed by these outlets, a malicious file was placed on the server that distributes updates for QBase, its ground-control software
→ The Bundeswehr grounded its Vector drones as a precaution; Quantum says it was the only customer to do so
→ Quantum shared no technical details and named no attacker; it is not clear how many customers installed the file
→ Quantum says the fleet is flying normally again; the Bundeswehr has not independently confirmed that

My take: your vendor's update server is part of your attack surface. I'd ask critical suppliers how updates are signed and checked, and stage their updates on a test system before production.

What to do: verify update signatures, stage vendor updates, list who can push code to you, and keep a rollback path.

items.take: Building and OT gear is the forgotten edge. I'd hunt for any controller reachable from the internet, including through 4G modems, before debating which firmware fixes what.

reel.hook: Six flaws. No login. Root. No patch.

segments.say: Six flaws. No login needed. Root. And no patch yet.
segments.show: Midnight Blue found six unpatched flaws in the Danfoss AK-SM800A store refrigeration controller. Five sit in web handlers that need no login and run as root (The Hacker News, 16 Nov).

segments.say: A researcher found them in supermarket fridge controllers in under an hour.
segments.show: Researcher Carlo Meijer found them in under an hour of manual review. Root code execution shown on firmware 3.3.0; same bugs in 5.3.2. Researchers say 5.4.0 doesn't fix them. No CVEs yet.

segments.say: No secure boot, so an implant could survive a factory reset.
segments.show: No secure boot: implants could survive factory resets and updates. BSI has no information on exploitation of these six flaws.

segments.say: Take the controller off the internet. Use a V P N.
segments.show: Remove internet exposure, including via 4G/5G modems. Remote access only over VPN. Check setpoints, defrost schedules and accounts for changes.

items.ig_caption:
Six flaws. No login needed. Root. And no patch yet. 🧊

What The Hacker News reported (16 Nov):
→ Midnight Blue found six unpatched flaws in the Danfoss AK-SM800A store refrigeration controller
→ Five are in web request handlers that need no login and run as root
→ Root code execution was shown on firmware 3.3.0; the same bugs are in 5.3.2, and researchers say 5.4.0 doesn't fix them
→ No secure boot, so implants could survive a factory reset
→ No CVEs or fix yet; Germany's BSI has no information on exploitation of these six flaws

My take: building and OT gear is the forgotten edge. I'd hunt for any controller reachable from the internet, including through 4G modems, before debating which firmware fixes what.

What to do: remove internet exposure, use VPN-only remote access, and check setpoints, defrost schedules and user accounts for unexplained changes.
